extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, and scholars interested in crime fiction (readers of encyclopedia overview)
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the crime fiction genre, its history, defining features, major subgenres, common tropes, and cultural variations — useful for writers and readers to recognise and produce works within the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central focus on criminal acts and investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives or fiction that centre on criminal acts and especially on the investigation, either by an amateur or a professional detective, of a crime, often a murder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crime fiction should place a crime and its investigation at the heart of the story; the investigation (by whomever) drives the plot. Example framing: detective story, murder mystery, police novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense and mystery as key elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense and mystery are key elements that are nearly ubiquitous to the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should cultivate uncertainty and tension about what happened, who is responsible, or what will happen next; pacing and withholding information are tools to achieve this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detective fiction (subgenre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subgenre in which an investigator or a detective—either professional, amateur, or retired—investigates a crime, often murder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative follows the detective's inquiry; focus is on clue-gathering, deduction, and the process of solving the crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cozy mystery (subgenre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subgenre of detective fiction in which profanity, sex, and violence are downplayed or treated humorously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone should be lightened; explicit content is minimized. Suitable settings often include small communities and amateur sleuths; emphasis on puzzle and character quirks over graphic realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whodunit (subgenre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex, plot-driven story in which the reader is provided with clues from which the identity of the perpetrator of the crime may be deduced before the solution is revealed at the end of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the narrative to fairly present clues and red herrings; maintain solvability while sustaining surprise. Examples: Golden Age puzzle mysteries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical whodunit (subgenre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whodunit set within a historical context; the setting of the story and the crime have some historical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical detail should be integrated into the mystery's mechanics and atmosphere; the period can shape the investigation methods and motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locked-room mystery (subgenre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specialized kind of whodunit in which the crime is committed under apparently impossible circumstances, such as a locked room which no intruder could have entered or left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The puzzle must present a credible impossibility and then provide a logical or ingenious explanation; misdirection and constrained settings are common devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-boiled / American hardboiled school
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguished by the unsentimental portrayal of violence and sex; the sleuth usually also confronts danger and engages in violence. Offers a more realistic social perspective to crime fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone is gritty and realist; protagonists may be morally ambiguous. Use of street-level detail, social context (e.g., Depression-era concerns), and stark prose are typical. Examples: Dashiell Hammett, Raymond Chandler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police procedural (subgenre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story in which the detective is a member of the police, thus the activities of a police force are usually convincingly depicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize institutional processes, teamwork, forensic and bureaucratic details; realism in investigative techniques and protocol is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forensic crime fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar to the police procedural; the investigator whom the reader follows is usually a medical examiner or pathologist who must use forensic evidence left on the body and at the crime scene to catch the killer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate depiction of forensic methods and chain-of-evidence concerns strengthens credibility; the science should inform plot solutions. Example: Patricia Cornwell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal thriller
rubrics_metrics.description: Major characters are lawyers and their employees, and they become involved in proving their cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot structure often revolves around courtroom strategy, legal ethics, evidentiary problems, and the lawyer's investigative role; legal procedure must be plausible and integral to stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spy novel / espionage
rubrics_metrics.description: Major characters are spies, usually working for an intelligence agency; includes political intrigue and moral ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize tradecraft, geopolitics, loyalty conflicts, and moral complexity; setting and realism vary from cold-war procedural to high-stakes global conspiracies. Examples: John le Carré.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caper story and criminal novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories told from the point of view of the criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the planning, execution, and fallout of crimes from the offender's perspective; tone may be humorous or sympathetic, and moral framing differs from detective-centred stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological thriller / psychological suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporates elements from detective fiction, as the protagonist must solve the mystery of the psychological conflict presented in these stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate on internal motives, unreliable perceptions, and mental states; suspense arises from psychological tension rather than only external clues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody / spoof
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses humor or sarcasm to lampoon aspects of crime fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerate genre conventions recognisably; the reader should recognise targeted tropes and the comedic inversion or commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime thriller (broad category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has central characters involved in crime, either in its investigation, as the perpetrator, or less commonly, a victim; often emphasizes pace and danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize tension, high stakes, and plot momentum; blend investigative elements with action and suspense to maintain reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nocturnal picaresque / city mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: Explores the secrets obscured in a city at nighttime; showcases the investigation of nefarious circumstances within a city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use urban setting and nocturnal atmosphere to reveal social undercurrents and hidden crimes; setting functions as a character that shapes plot and mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic mystery and paranormal blends
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporates paranormal activity into the story, including other beings such as ghosts and vampires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend supernatural elements with investigative structure; decide whether the paranormal is literal or psychological and keep narrative consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gallows and criminal confession subgenres
rubrics_metrics.description: Gallows subgenre: story revolves around the hanging of potential criminals. Criminal confession: character motives and admittance are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gallows fiction centers execution and its moral/ethical dimensions; confession narratives foreground motive and internal justification rather than outside detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Age conventions (puzzle-first storytelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Golden Age novels commonly prioritized the allure of exploring mysteries in the plot over in-depth character development; clues may be analyzed by the protagonist in tandem with the reader, generating possibility of understanding the narrative before it is revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing in this mode, foreground fair-play clueing, structured puzzles, and an emphasis on logical deduction. Examples: Agatha Christie, Dorothy L. Sayers; reference to Ronald Knox's 'Detective Story Decalogue' as era rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common tropes and narrative practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Many crime fiction works often begin when the crime has already occurred; usage of serial killers, unreliable narrators, plot-puzzle formula, detectives, and dark real-life themes (slavery, organised crime) are common. Works frequently draw from cultural and legal realities of their origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should decide whether to start in medias res (after crime) or show the crime; choose tropes deliberately (e.g., unreliable narrator) and be aware of cultural specificity — for instance, Spanish crime fiction emphasised corruption and inept police, Chinese crime fiction has its own historical contours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of realism and use of legal/social systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspiration can be drawn from the legal system around the world, with varying degrees of realism; some writers use detective formats to critique institutions, portray imperfect detectives, or leave crimes unsolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the level of procedural accuracy and institutional critique appropriate to the story; realistic depiction of police, courts, and forensic methods increases plausibility, while postmodern/antidetective works may subvert expectations by leaving ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement via fair clueing vs. spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Some traditions (e.g., Golden Age) present clues so readers can deduce the solution; others prioritize spectacle and deduction performed by the detective for the reader's entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between offering solvable puzzles and dramatic reveals — choose whether the reader should be able to 'beat' the detective or be led through the investigative spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pseudonyms and market/practical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors sometimes publish under pseudonyms either for privacy or to avoid market baggage; pseudonymous practices have historical and commercial rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider pseudonym use if shifting subgenre/style or resetting market expectations; note that author identity can affect reader reception and publisher decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological/therapeutic impact on readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime fiction can provide mediated witnessing and escapism, act as 'distraction therapy', and may improve mental health or help cope with life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting tone and content, be aware of the potential bibliotherapeutic effect; balancing distressing material with narrative distance can make works more broadly accessible.
